ann_121.text: Through this part, the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less is lowest at about 47 years and higher either side: for a typical person it clearly falls from about 84% at 22 years to about 55% at 58 years.

For most people the chance is lowest at about 47 years, but for the 26 people born in Thailand the model clearly treats age the other way: the same change in age raises the predicted chance steadily from about 66% to about 85%.
Being born in Ireland rather than elsewhere lowers it from about 63% to about 26% through this part (on the training data only).

ann_122.text: Through this part, capital gains clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less slowly at first, then faster, from about 63% at none to about 12% at $6,849, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower.
The drop is slightly larger for people born outside the Netherlands and Ecuador (about 63% to about 9%) than for the 37 people born in Ecuador (about 71% to about 15%).
Being born in Ecuador on its own slightly raises the predicted chance through this part (it stays at about 63%).

ann_123.text: This part acts on 1,993 of 39,073 people in the training data (5%), and 234 of them had an income of $50,000 or less.

Through it, capital gains clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, nothing until about 4883 US dollars, then steadily: from about 63% at none to about 56% at $6,849.

For the typical person it acts on (a 44-year-old White man married to a civilian spouse, born in the United States, with a bachelor's degree, a professional specialty job in the private sector, 44 hours a week and $7,688 in capital gains), it slightly lowers the predicted chance, which stays at about 1%.
For that person, a 9th-grade education or being born in Jamaica, Nicaragua or the Philippines slightly raises the predicted chance through this part (it stays at about 1%).
Being born in Scotland does the same, slightly raising it, but the model has little data on this (16 people).

The drop with capital gains is slightly larger for people born outside Jamaica, Nicaragua, the Philippines and Scotland (about 63% to about 9%) than for people born in Jamaica (about 71% to about 16%).

ann_124.text: This part acts on the 3,034 of 39,073 people in the training data (8%) who are self-employed without incorporation, and 2,215 of them had an income of $50,000 or less.
Through it, being self-employed without incorporation raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to about 77% (on the training data only).

For the typical person it acts on (a 44-year-old White man married to a civilian spouse, born in the United States, a high-school graduate doing craft or repair work, self-employed without incorporation, working 40 hours a week), it raises the predicted chance from about 60% to about 74% (on the training data only).

ann_125.text: This part acts on 31,364 of 39,073 people in the training data (80%), and 25,290 of them had an income of $50,000 or less.

Through it, more working hours clearly lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily up to about 50 hours a week, then no further: for a typical person, going from 17 to 99 hours moves it from about 85% to about 51%.
Working 55 rather than 24 hours a week therefore clearly lowers it from about 79% to about 51%, with no further change past that point.

For the typical person it acts on (a 36-year-old White man married to a civilian spouse, born in the United States, a high-school graduate in an administrative or clerical job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week), it clearly raises the predicted chance from about 62% to about 73%.

ann_126.text: Through this part, being another relative in the household clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to about 82%.
Having some college as the highest education raises it only slightly, to about 64% (on the training data only).

ann_127.text: Through this part, a preschool education clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to about 88%.
Being born in Trinidad and Tobago raises it to about 92%, and being born in Yugoslavia lowers it to about 33% (on the training data only; 22 and 21 people).
State government work and protective service jobs lower it only slightly (it stays at about 63%), on the training data only.

ann_128.text: Through this part, compared with being born in the United States, being born in Colombia raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to above 99%, in 'South' (as recorded) to about 89%, in Peru to about 87%, in China to about 84% and in the Dominican Republic to about 81% (on the training data only).
Being born in Portugal lowers it to about 38%, in England to about 52% and in Canada to about 58% (on the training data only).
Being born in Haiti (about 74%), Iran (about 70%) or one of the countries this part does not tell apart (about 71%) also raises it (on the training data only).
Being born in Scotland raises it to about 94% and being born in Cambodia lowers it to about 56%, but the model has little data on this (16 and 19 people), on the training data only.
Being born in Poland, Germany or Hungary raises it only slightly (to about 68%, 65% and 68%), on the training data only, and for Hungary the model has little data on this (16 people).

ann_129.text: Through this part, a higher education level and capital losses both clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily: from about 84% at 7 to about 35% at 13 on the 1-16 education scale, and from about 63% at no capital losses to about 31% at $1,887.

Compared with being married to a civilian spouse, it clearly gives a higher chance to people who are divorced (about 95%), widowed (about 91%) or in a marital status other than married, divorced or widowed (about 97%), and below 1% to the 29 people married to a member of the armed forces.

Compared with a professional specialty, farming or fishing (about 87%), other service jobs (about 85%), handlers or cleaners (about 83%), machine operators or inspectors (about 78%), a missing occupation (about 78%) and the occupations it does not tell apart (about 71%) clearly raise it, and executive or managerial jobs clearly lower it to about 56%.
Being a woman (about 74%) or someone's own child in the household (about 74%) clearly raises it, and being a wife clearly lowers it to about 41%.

Protective service and technical support jobs slightly lower it (to about 58% and 59%), being listed in the household as unmarried slightly lowers it (to about 62%), and sales jobs slightly raise it (to about 67%).

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients

confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points

ann_122.text: This changes the prediction only slightly: for a typical person, capital gains going from 0 US dollars to 6849 US dollars moves the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to about 9% if country of birth is something other than the Netherlands, Ecuador, and from about 71% to about 15% if the country of birth is Ecuador (it moves slowly at first, then faster for people with country of birth other than the Netherlands, Ecuador).
